title: Hash Tables
tagline: The O(1) lookup superpower — and exactly what can go wrong when the math breaks down.

sections.content:
A hash table is the data structure behind JavaScript's `{}` objects and `Map`, Python's `dict`, Ruby's `Hash`, and Java's `HashMap`. It achieves **O(1) average-case** lookup, insertion, and deletion by converting a key into an array index with a **hash function** — transforming "find this key" into "read this array slot". That is an extraordinary capability: no matter how many items are stored, finding one takes roughly the same time. It is the reason a Python dictionary with ten million entries looks up a key just as fast as one with ten.

The catch — and what every senior interviewer wants to know you understand deeply — is that O(1) is an **average**, not a guarantee. Hash collisions, poor hash functions, and excessive load can degrade performance to O(n). The difference between using a hash table and truly understanding one is grasping why collisions are inevitable, how they are resolved, and what can break the amortised analysis.

Hash tables are also the key to unlocking dozens of classic algorithm problems. Two Sum, group anagram, LRU cache, word frequency counting — all become elegant one-pass solutions when you reach for a hash map. But to use them confidently in high-stakes situations, you need to understand the machinery under the hood: the hash function, the collision resolution strategy, the load factor, rehashing, and the rare worst-case scenarios that interviewers love to probe.

In this chapter we will build a hash table from scratch, explore both major collision strategies, understand the amortised cost analysis, and look at real-world implications from Hash DoS attacks to language runtime design decisions.

sections.title: A Filing Cabinet with a Magic Labeller
sections.content:
Imagine a filing cabinet with 100 numbered drawers. You have a magic labeller: feed it a name ('alice') and it always spits out the same drawer number (37). To store Alice's record you put it in drawer 37. To retrieve it later you run the labeller again — no searching required, O(1).

The labeller never looks at existing drawers. It does not care whether drawer 37 already has something in it. It only computes the number from the name using a fixed rule. That is the hash function: a pure, deterministic computation that converts input to a number.

But sometimes two different names map to the same drawer number (a **collision**). You handle this either by **chaining** — keeping a growing list of items inside each drawer — or by **open addressing** — checking the next available drawer when your target is full. The magic labeller must be fast and distribute names evenly across all 100 drawers. If half the documents pile up in drawer 3, your O(1) promise breaks down and you are effectively scanning a list.

The "magic" also breaks if the labeller is predictable: a malicious person who figures out the labelling rule can send you thousands of names that all map to drawer 3, creating a deliberately degraded O(n) lookup — a Hash DoS attack.

sections.title: The Hash Function: Turning Keys into Indices
sections.content:
A **hash function** maps an arbitrary key to a non-negative integer (the **hash code**), which is then reduced modulo the bucket count to get the array index. It must satisfy three properties:

1. **Deterministic** — the same key must always produce the same hash code. Without this, a key stored with hash X might be looked up with hash Y, and the entry would never be found.
2. **Fast to compute** — ideally O(1) or O(key length). A hash function that takes O(n) time to compute destroys the O(1) lookup promise.
3. **Uniform distribution** — outputs should spread evenly across all possible indices. Clustering keys into a few buckets creates long chains, degrading lookup toward O(n).

For **integer keys**, a common hash function is simply the key itself modulo the bucket count, sometimes combined with a bit-mixing step to handle poor input distributions. For **string keys**, a classic approach is the **polynomial rolling hash**: accumulate `h = h * PRIME + charCode` for each character, using a prime multiplier (31 or 37 are popular choices) because prime multipliers spread bits into more positions and reduce the chance of accidental collisions.

The choice of prime matters. Using 31 (as Java's `String.hashCode()` does) means `hash('abc') = 'a'*31² + 'b'*31 + 'c'`. The prime base causes small changes in the input (different characters) to ripple through many positions of the output, a property called **avalanche behaviour**. Modern production hash functions like **MurmurHash3**, **FNV-1a**, and **CityHash** extend this idea with bitwise mixing steps specifically designed for uniform distribution across real-world key distributions.

Critically, hash codes and array indices are **not** the same thing. The hash code can be any 32-bit or 64-bit integer; the array index must be in `[0, bucketCount)`. The modulo step bridges them: `index = Math.abs(hashCode) % bucketCount`. If the hash code is negative (which can happen with 32-bit overflow in JavaScript), the absolute value is taken first.

flowchart TD

  B --> C["hashCode: 93029210"]
  C --> D["index = hashCode % 16\n= 93029210 % 16 = 10"]
  D --> E["buckets[10] = value"]
sections.caption: Polynomial rolling hash in detail: each character of the string is folded into the running hash with a prime multiplier, spreading input variation across the output bits.

sections.title: Collisions: Why They Are Inevitable
sections.content:
A **collision** occurs when two different keys produce the same array index. Collisions are not a bug — they are mathematically unavoidable. This follows directly from the **pigeonhole principle**: if you store more items than there are buckets, at least two items must share a bucket. But even before you reach capacity, the **birthday paradox** tells us collisions become likely much sooner than intuition suggests.

The birthday paradox: in a group of just 23 people, there is a 50% chance two share a birthday (365 possible days). Analogously, with `m` buckets, collisions become likely after inserting roughly `√(2m)` items — much less than `m`. This means collisions are not edge cases; they happen constantly in real hash tables and the collision strategy is always active, not occasional.

Given this, a correct hash table implementation **must** have a collision resolution strategy from day one. There are two major families:

**Separate chaining** stores a secondary data structure (linked list, dynamic array, or even a small tree) at each bucket. Multiple keys mapping to the same index simply append to the chain. Lookup walks the chain comparing keys until it finds the target. Chain length depends on load: with a low load factor, chains rarely exceed 1–2 elements, keeping lookup at O(1).

**Open addressing** stores all key-value pairs directly inside the bucket array — no separate lists. On collision, it **probes** a sequence of alternative slots. The three standard probe sequences are: **linear probing** (try index+1, +2, +3...), **quadratic probing** (try index+1², +2², +3²...), and **double hashing** (try index + k*hash2(key) for k=1, 2, 3...). Open addressing uses memory more efficiently (no pointer overhead) and has better cache locality — all data lives in one contiguous array. But it suffers from **primary clustering** (linear probing) where full regions form and probe sequences keep overlapping, and it becomes catastrophically slow at high load factors.

sections.caption: Chaining appends a linked list at each bucket — simple and robust at high load. Open addressing probes the same array — cache-friendly but requires care on deletion and struggles above 70% load.

sections.title: Open Addressing: The Tombstone Problem
sections.content:
Open addressing has a subtle complexity around **deletion**. Suppose keys A and B both hash to index 5. A is inserted at slot 5, B is inserted (via linear probing) at slot 6. Now you delete A by simply clearing slot 5. Later you look up B: hash to 5, slot 5 is empty — lookup returns "not found", which is **wrong**. B is at slot 6 but the probe was short-circuited by the empty slot.

The solution is **tombstone markers**: deleted slots are marked as "deleted" rather than "empty". During lookup, a tombstone means "keep probing"; during insert, a tombstone means "this slot is usable". Tombstones degrade performance over time — a table with many tombstones has long probe sequences. Periodic full rehashes clear tombstones.

This complexity is one reason **separate chaining is more commonly used** in language standard libraries. Java's `HashMap`, Python's dict (which actually uses open addressing with a custom probe sequence based on perturbation), and JavaScript's `Map` each make different trade-offs. Python's `dict` (CPython implementation) uses open addressing with pseudorandom probing specifically because it performs better for Python's typical small-to-medium dictionary sizes and avoids the pointer overhead of chaining.

For interview purposes: know both strategies, be able to describe the tombstone issue, and know that chaining is generally simpler and more robust at high load.

sections.title: Load Factor and Rehashing
sections.content:
The **load factor** (λ = items stored ÷ bucket count) is the single most important parameter controlling hash table performance. It measures how full the table is. As load factor rises, chains grow longer (for chaining) or probe sequences lengthen (for open addressing), and average lookup time creeps toward O(n).

The standard solution is **rehashing**: when load factor exceeds a threshold, allocate a larger bucket array (typically 2× the current size) and reinsert every existing key-value pair. All indices change because the modulus changes — you cannot simply copy the array. This is O(n) and proportional to the current size.

Why does rehashing not ruin the O(1) amortised average? Because rehashing happens **exponentially rarely**. With the 2× growth strategy:
- You rehash after inserting item n (when table fills)
- The next rehash happens after inserting 2n more items
- The one after that after 4n more
- Total rehash work: n + 2n + 4n + ... = O(n) summed over the entire sequence of n insertions
- Amortised cost per insert: O(n)/n = O(1)

This is the same amortised analysis as dynamic arrays (like JavaScript's arrays or Java's `ArrayList`). The key insight: you pay an occasional large cost, but so infrequently that the average over all operations stays O(1).

Typical load factor thresholds:
- Separate chaining: 0.75 (Java's `HashMap` default)
- Open addressing: 0.5 (higher load causes severe clustering)

Below the threshold, average chain length stays below 1 for chaining, and probe sequences stay short for open addressing. The load factor is a tunable trade-off: lower threshold = faster lookups but more memory; higher threshold = more memory-efficient but slower.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The `#hash` method uses the polynomial rolling hash: starting at 0, it multiplies by 31 and adds each character's code point. The `>>> 0` operator coerces to an unsigned 32-bit integer, preventing negative values that would produce negative modulo results in JS. The `#rehash` method doubles the array and calls `set()` on each existing entry — this is safe because `set()` already handles both insert and update, and the new indices are computed automatically by the updated capacity.

sections.title: Worst Case O(n): When the Math Breaks Down
sections.content:
The O(1) average case assumes the hash function distributes keys **uniformly** across buckets. When this assumption fails — whether by accident or by design — the hash table degrades toward O(n) lookup.

**Accidental worst case**: All input keys happen to have the same hash modulo the bucket count. Example: if your table has 16 buckets and your hash function returns values that are multiples of 16 for your specific input, all items land in bucket 0. Every lookup must scan the entire chain. For most real-world inputs with a good hash function this is astronomically unlikely, but it can happen with pathological inputs (e.g., all-zero strings, or strings whose character values sum to the same multiple of the bucket count).

**Deliberate worst case — Hash DoS**: If an attacker knows (or can guess) your hash function, they can craft a set of inputs that all collide at the same bucket. Sending these as HTTP request parameters causes your server to spend O(n) time processing each request instead of O(1), effectively creating a CPU-based denial-of-service attack with a small number of carefully chosen keys.

This attack was publicly demonstrated in 2011 against PHP, Java, and Ruby web servers. The fix adopted by essentially all modern runtimes is **hash seed randomisation**: at process startup, a random 64-bit value is generated and incorporated into the hash function (e.g., `hash = hashWithSeed(key, seed)` where seed is random). Even if an attacker knows your hash algorithm, they cannot predict outputs without knowing the runtime seed, so they cannot craft colliding keys. JavaScript V8, Python (since 3.3 with `PYTHONHASHSEED`), and Java (since Java 7u6) all do this.

The implication for interviews: when asked about worst-case hash table performance, always say "O(n) when all keys collide" and optionally mention Hash DoS as a real security consequence.

sections.title: Big-O Summary and Comparison with Other Structures
sections.content:
Here is where hash tables sit relative to other fundamental data structures:

**Hash table** — O(1) average lookup/insert/delete, O(n) worst case. No ordering guarantees. Keys must be hashable.

**Binary search tree (balanced)** — O(log n) lookup/insert/delete, guaranteed. Keys must be comparable. Supports ordered traversal.

**Sorted array** — O(log n) lookup (binary search), O(n) insert/delete (shifting). Supports ordered traversal and range queries.

**Unsorted array / linked list** — O(n) lookup, O(1) insert at end. No overhead, but no fast lookup.

The hash table wins decisively on lookup and insert speed when you do not need ordering. The trade-off is that you cannot efficiently ask "give me all keys between X and Y" (a range query) — that requires a sorted structure. You also cannot iterate in sorted order without a separate sort step.

In practice, language standard libraries often combine both: Python's `dict` preserves **insertion order** (since Python 3.7+) but is still a hash table — it iterates in insertion order, not sorted order. JavaScript's `Map` also preserves insertion order. If you need sorted iteration, use a balanced BST (Java's `TreeMap`, C++'s `std::map`), which sacrifices O(1) average lookups for O(log n) guaranteed and sorted traversal.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: All four patterns share the same core insight: trade O(n) extra space to convert an O(n²) nested-loop problem into an O(n) single-pass solution. Two Sum is the canonical example — storing seen values turns a brute-force double loop into a single scan. Group anagrams uses the sorted characters as a canonical key, collapsing all anagrams into a single group. Notice the use of `Map` throughout — never plain `{}`, which could shadow keys like 'constructor'.

sections.title: Choosing Keys: What Can Be Hashed
sections.content:
Not every data type can be a hash table key. There is a fundamental rule: **if two values are considered equal, they must produce the same hash code**. This is the hash contract, and violating it silently breaks the table.

In JavaScript, object identity (not equality) determines hash keys. Two distinct object references with identical contents are considered different keys:

```js
const m = new Map();
m.set({x: 1}, 'A');
m.set({x: 1}, 'B');  // different object reference!
console.log(m.size); // 2, not 1
```

This is correct behaviour — JavaScript's `Map` uses reference equality for object keys. But it means you cannot directly use objects as hash map keys when you want value equality. Workarounds: serialize to string (e.g., `JSON.stringify(key)`), or use a custom identity scheme.

In Java, this principle is explicit: `hashCode()` and `equals()` are contract-linked. If you override `equals()`, you **must** override `hashCode()` consistently. Java's `String` overrides both correctly: two strings with identical characters will have the same `hashCode()` and be `equals()`. But plain Java objects inherit `Object.hashCode()` which returns an identity-based value — two objects with identical fields will have different hash codes unless you override.

Python enforces the same contract. Mutable objects (`list`, `dict`, `set`) are not hashable by default because mutating an object after inserting it would change its hash code, breaking the table's ability to find it. Only immutable types (`str`, `int`, `tuple` of hashable elements, `frozenset`) are hashable in Python. This is why you get `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'` when you try to use a list as a dictionary key.

**Key rule for interviews**: Only use **immutable** values as hash table keys. In JavaScript, use primitives (strings, numbers, booleans) or convert complex keys to a canonical string representation.

flowchart LR

then hash(a) == hash(b)"]
  A --> C["If hash(a) != hash(b)

sections.caption: The hash contract: equal keys must produce equal hash codes. The converse is not required — equal hash codes do not mean equal keys (that is a collision). Violating the contract silently corrupts the table.

sections.content: **Brief history**: Hash tables were independently invented in the early 1950s. H.P. Luhn at IBM described a hashing scheme in 1953, and W.W. Peterson published the first formal analysis of open addressing in 1957. The term 'hash' likely derives from the idea of 'hashing up' or mixing the key to produce a dispersed value — the same word used in cooking and random mixing. Donald Knuth's *The Art of Computer Programming* (Vol. 3, 1973) provided the first rigorous mathematical analysis of collision resolution strategies and load factor effects. Python's dictionary, often cited as one of the best hash table implementations, was significantly optimised by Raymond Hettinger in 2012 with the compact dictionary design, later becoming the default in CPython 3.6.

**Interview traps and insights to know cold:**

- Always say O(1) **average** — never just O(1). Interviewers at senior levels will specifically probe whether you know the difference.
- Prefer `Map` over `{}` for hash-table patterns: `Map` supports any key type (objects, arrays, numbers), guarantees insertion-order iteration, exposes `.size` directly, and avoids prototype-chain key shadowing (`'constructor'`, `'toString'` are valid `Map` keys but problematic in `{}`).
- When designing a hash table with object keys, convert to a canonical string with `JSON.stringify` — but beware key ordering: `{a:1,b:2}` and `{b:2,a:1}` stringify differently. Sort keys first.
- Rehashing cost is **amortised O(1) per insert** — understand why (the doubling argument) before claiming it.
- Hash DoS is a real attack: always mention hash seed randomisation when discussing hash table security.
- The birthday paradox explains why collisions happen at ~√(2m) inserts, not m inserts — tables need collision handling from the very start.

items: A **hash function** converts a key to an array index in O(1), giving average-case O(1) lookup, insertion, and deletion — no matter how many entries the table holds.

**Collisions are inevitable** (pigeonhole principle); the two main resolution strategies are **separate chaining** (linked list at each bucket) and **open addressing** (probe for the next free slot in the array).

The **load factor** (items ÷ buckets) is the key performance dial. When it exceeds the threshold (0.75 for chaining, 0.5 for open addressing), **rehashing** doubles the array and reinserts all entries — O(n) but amortised O(1) per insert because it happens exponentially rarely.
Worst-case is **O(n)** when all keys collide. This can be triggered deliberately (Hash DoS attack), which is why modern runtimes randomise the hash seed at startup.

The **hash contract** is critical: equal keys must produce equal hash codes. Mutable keys (lists, dicts in Python; objects in Java without overriding `hashCode`) violate this contract and silently break the table.
Classic interview problems — **Two Sum, Group Anagrams, Frequency Counter, First Unique Character** — all reduce from O(n²) brute force to O(n) by trading space for an O(1) lookup structure.
Use JavaScript's `Map` over `{}` for hash-table patterns: any key type, no prototype pollution, guaranteed insertion-order iteration, and a built-in `size` property.

quiz.question: What is the average-case time complexity of looking up a key in a well-implemented hash table?
options: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)
quiz.explanation: A hash function converts the key to an array index in constant time. With a good hash function and a load factor below the threshold, the lookup touches only one bucket — O(1) average. This is an average, not a guarantee; worst-case is O(n) when all keys collide.

quiz.question: When does a hash table degrade to O(n) lookup?
options: When the table is completely empty
When all keys hash to the same bucket
When the load factor drops below 0.5
When the hash function uses a prime multiplier
quiz.explanation: If all keys collide at one bucket, every lookup must scan the entire chain — O(n). This is the worst case and can be triggered intentionally with chosen keys (Hash DoS), which is why modern runtimes randomise the hash seed.

quiz.question: What is the load factor of a hash table, and why does it matter?
options: The number of hash collisions per operation — a low count means fewer rehashes
The ratio of stored items to total buckets — exceeding the threshold triggers rehashing to restore O(1) performance
The maximum key length the table supports — longer keys require a larger table
The time it takes to compute the hash function — shorter hash time means better load handling
quiz.explanation: Load factor λ = n (items stored) ÷ m (bucket count). As λ rises, chains grow (for chaining) or probe sequences lengthen (for open addressing), degrading lookup. Exceeding the threshold (typically 0.75 for chaining) triggers rehashing — doubling the bucket array to restore O(1) average performance.

quiz.question: In separate chaining collision resolution, what is stored at each bucket?
options: A single value — the first key that hashed there
A linked list (or array) of all key-value pairs that hashed to that bucket
The hash code of the most recently inserted key
A pointer to the next empty bucket in the array
quiz.explanation: Separate chaining keeps a secondary data structure (linked list, dynamic array, or small tree) at each bucket. Multiple keys hashing to the same index are appended. Lookup walks the chain comparing keys — O(1) average when chains stay short due to low load factor.

quiz.question: Why is the amortised cost of hash table insertion O(1) even though rehashing costs O(n)?
options: Rehashing only moves half the entries, so it takes O(n/2) which simplifies to O(1)
Rehashing costs O(n) but happens exponentially rarely — the 2x growth strategy means total rehash work over n inserts is O(n), giving O(1) per insert
Rehashing is performed in the background by a separate thread and does not count toward the insert cost
The O(n) rehash cost is paid by the delete operation, not the insert operation
quiz.explanation: With 2x growth, rehash events happen after n, 2n, 4n, ... insertions. Total rehash work = n + 2n + 4n + ... = O(n) across n insertions. Dividing by n gives O(1) amortised per insert — the same analysis as dynamic array doubling.

quiz.question: What is the tombstone problem in open addressing hash tables?
options: When the hash function produces hash codes larger than the table size
When deleted slots are left empty, causing lookup probes to stop early and miss valid entries in later slots
When the table runs out of memory and must evict the least recently used entry
When two keys produce identical hash codes and cannot be distinguished
quiz.explanation: In open addressing, if a deleted slot is cleared to empty, a probe sequence will stop at that slot and incorrectly report 'not found' for any entry that was originally placed past the deleted slot. Tombstone markers ('deleted but not empty') keep probe sequences going, at the cost of degraded performance over time.

quiz.question: Why should you prefer `Map` over a plain `{}` object for hash-table patterns in JavaScript?
options: Map is O(log n) for all operations whereas {} is O(n)
Map supports any key type (objects, numbers, functions) and avoids prototype-chain key shadowing issues
Plain objects are limited to 100 entries by the JavaScript specification
Map automatically sorts keys by insertion time for O(1) ordered access
quiz.explanation: Map accepts any value as a key (objects, numbers, booleans, etc.) and is free of the Object prototype chain that can shadow keys like 'constructor' or 'toString'. Map also preserves insertion order, exposes a built-in `size` property, and has clean iteration via `entries()`, `keys()`, and `values()` methods.

quiz.question: Which property must a hash function satisfy for the hash table to work correctly?
options: It must produce a different index for every unique key (no collisions ever)
It must be deterministic: the same key must always produce the same hash code
It must run in O(log n) time relative to the number of stored entries
It must distribute keys in alphabetical order across the bucket array
quiz.explanation: Determinism is the non-negotiable requirement: same key → same hash, always. Without it, a key stored with hash X cannot be found because a subsequent lookup might return hash Y. Collisions (two different keys → same hash) are expected and handled, but inconsistent hashing for the same key is fatal.

quiz.question: What is Hash DoS, and what is the standard defense against it?
options: A denial-of-service attack via SHA-256 collisions; defended by switching to SHA-512
An attacker crafts keys that all collide at one bucket, degrading O(1) to O(n) per request; defended by randomising the hash seed at startup
A memory exhaustion attack by sending huge hash codes; defended by capping the maximum key length
A race condition in multi-threaded hash table access; defended by adding mutex locks per bucket
quiz.explanation: Hash DoS exploits predictable hash functions: an attacker sends keys crafted to all collide, making each lookup O(n) and exhausting CPU. Modern runtimes (V8, CPython since 3.3, Java since 7u6) randomise the hash seed at process startup so attackers cannot predict which keys collide.

quiz.question: The Two Sum problem asks: given an array and a target, return indices of two numbers that sum to the target. What is the optimal approach using a hash table?
options: Sort the array first (O(n log n)), then use two pointers walking inward
Nest two loops over all pairs and check each sum — O(n²) with no extra space
For each element x, look up (target - x) in a hash map of previously seen values — O(n) time and space
Build a min-heap from the array and extract pairs until the sum matches — O(n log n)
quiz.explanation: One pass through the array: for each element x at index i, compute complement = target - x and check the map. If found, return [map.get(complement), i]. Otherwise store x → i. This is O(n) time and O(n) space — the standard hash table trade-off of space for speed, converting a brute-force O(n²) search into a single linear scan.
